headline: Why a museum is a harder contract than the hotels that built Diriyah's programme
deck: SAMoCA's SAR 1.84bn award puts 77,428 square metres of cultural building into a supply chain built for residential and hospitality volume.
excerpt: Diriyah Company's SAR 1.84bn ($490m) award for the Saudi Arabia Museum of Contemporary Art goes to a joint venture of AlBawani and Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia. The building is a different kind of construction risk from the hotels and homes that have carried Diriyah's programme, and the joint venture is how the market has learned to price it.
content:
Diriyah Company has let the Saudi Arabia Museum of Contemporary Art to a joint venture of AlBawani Holding and Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia at SAR 1.84bn ($490m). The number is not the interesting part of the award. What the building asks of its contractors is, because a museum of 77,428 square metres of built-up area and 45,252 square metres of gross floor area is a different kind of job from the residential and hospitality packages that have carried Diriyah's programme so far. The award itself, its place in the developer's $29bn of let contracts and the hotel and retail packages around it are set out in BrentDesk's report on the contract.

Cultural buildings carry a high value per square metre against residential or commercial work, and the difficulty is not in the volume of concrete. It sits in tolerances, in the environmental control a collection requires, and in the fact that the finishes are the product rather than a covering over it. Gallery spaces need stable temperature and humidity, controlled daylight, structural provision for loads that arrive after handover and acoustic separation between rooms, and none of that can be resolved late, because the systems are buried in the fabric of the building.

That makes the schedule less forgiving than the headline value suggests. On a residential block a delayed finishing package moves the handover. On a museum, a services coordination error can require opening completed work, and the commissioning period before a collection can be installed is measured in months of stable running rather than in days of testing. Diriyah Company has not published a completion date, which is unsurprising for a building of this kind.

The joint venture is how the market prices that risk. AlBawani is among the larger Saudi civil contractors and holds other Diriyah work, including a share of the Wadi Safar hotels package. Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia is the Kingdom's arm of the Egyptian group, which has built a Saudi business rather than working the market from Cairo, a pattern several regional contractors have followed as the pipeline concentrated here. Pairing a domestic balance sheet and labour base with a regional group's experience of complex, low-repetition structures is the standard structure for work of this size, and it is how most of Diriyah's larger packages have been let.

The supply chain the contract reaches into is narrower than a district's. A museum needs facade specialists, museum services engineers, conservation-grade mechanical and electrical subcontractors and finishing trades with a reference list in cultural work rather than in volume delivery. In a market where awards have been getting larger and local content is audited, those trades are the part of the Saudi supply base with the least depth, which is one reason a landmark building goes to two contractors rather than one.

The contract also marks where Diriyah's programme has reached. Its early packages were dominated by enabling works, infrastructure and the residential and hospitality assets that underpin the commercial case. Letting a major cultural building means the destination content, the reason a visitor travels to Diriyah rather than the accommodation that holds them there, is now being procured in earnest. The Museums Commission's intent for SAMoCA to collect, research and display Saudi modern and contemporary art gives the building a programme that has to be designed in from the start rather than fitted out at the end.

For the wider contracting market, the award is one of the more substantial single-building contracts let in the Kingdom this year, at a point when monthly award values have been uneven. It is also a reminder that the giga-project pipeline is no longer uniformly about scale. A 77,000 square metre museum is a fraction of the floor area in a single residential district, but it demands more specialised work per square metre than almost anything else on the masterplan.
